description: Width tiers for Year 10 Geography — ACARA v9. Covers all 13 descriptors across Knowledge and Understanding (K01–K08) and Geographical Inquiry Skills (S01–S06) strands. Generated from ACARA elaborations using width_generation_prompt v1.0.
subject: Geography

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement with the descriptor's command term — the fewest contexts or phenomena a student must engage with to genuinely satisfy what the descriptor requires. Not what is easy or convenient, but the non-negotiable floor.
width_notes.typical_width: Full engagement with the descriptor's scope as ACARA intended — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a class that has properly worked through the descriptor would have done. Not every elaboration covered, but the spirit and scope of the descriptor met.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, contexts, or task types — not harder versions of the same context. Each item in the wider array is a discrete direction that genuinely broadens the range of cases or contexts a student has engaged with.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are used as source data to identify the range of intended contexts and phenomena. They are examples, not a required sequence. Elaborations ground typical_width and inform wider items; First Nations elaborations are treated as default wider directions.

AC9HG10K01.minimum_width: Describe at least two types of human-induced environmental change using one studied context, and explain sustainability in relation to at least one environmental function.
AC9HG10K01.typical_width: Explain the nature of human-induced environmental change including water and atmospheric pollution, loss of biodiversity, and degradation of land and aquatic environments across a range of examples; explain sustainability across resource, service and spiritual environmental functions; identify and explain tensions between conflicting perspectives of individuals, communities, businesses and governments on sustainable practices.
wider: Investigate a complex multi-cause environmental change case (e.g. Murray-Darling Basin, Great Barrier Reef) tracing interactions between pollution, biodiversity loss and land degradation simultaneously
Compare contested definitions of sustainability (weak vs strong, anthropocentric vs ecocentric) and evaluate their implications for what counts as adequate management
Analyse a specific governance dispute (e.g. community vs developer, state vs federal) tracing how institutional power determines which perspectives on sustainability prevail
Examine international frameworks (UN SDGs, planetary boundaries) as formal attempts to operationalise sustainability and evaluate their adequacy
elaborations: identifying tensions between the conflicting perspectives of individuals, communities and governments on the use of sustainable practices

explaining the nature of human-induced environmental changes (for example, water and atmospheric pollution; loss of biodiversity; degradation of land and aquatic environments) and the challenge they pose for sustainability
discussing the concept of sustainability in relation to environmental functions and identifying tensions between the conflicting perspectives of communities, businesses and government

AC9HG10K02.minimum_width: Define human-centred and earth-centred world views and describe one management approach associated with each; compare two different stakeholder perspectives on the causes of one environmental issue.
AC9HG10K02.typical_width: Explain the philosophical basis and practical implications of human-centred and earth-centred world views; compare differences in people's views about causes of an environmental issue of personal, national and global importance; discuss whether environmental change is necessarily a problem requiring management and explain people's choices of management methods.
wider: Investigate intermediate world views (stewardship ethics, biocentric ethics) that complicate the binary, evaluating how each positions human responsibility differently
Examine how legal frameworks encode world views — rights of nature legislation in Ecuador or New Zealand vs resource-rights regimes in Australia
Analyse media coverage of an environmental issue from outlets reflecting different world views, identifying how framing choices encode particular world view positions
Compare how Indigenous world views — including First Nations Australian relational ontologies — differ from both human-centred and earth-centred Western frameworks
elaborations: discussing the influence of people's environmental world views (human-centred and earth-centred) regarding environmental management
comparing differences in peoples' views about the causes of an environmental issue of personal, national and global importance
discussing whether environmental change is necessarily a problem that should be managed and explaining people's choices of methods for managing or responding to environmental changes

AC9HG10K03.minimum_width: Define custodial responsibility and explain its basis in cultural values for at least one Country/Place; describe the role of First Nations Rangers in managing that Country/Place with reference to at least one cultural practice.
AC9HG10K03.typical_width: Explain the influence of cultural values (continuity of practices, obligations to Country/Place, land tenure) on how First Nations Australians manage environments in different regions; describe the role of First Nations Rangers and the integration of cultural knowledge in management; explain First Nations models of sustainability including fire management, land care, species protection and capacity building and how these contribute to conservation.
wider: Compare custodial responsibility frameworks in different First Nations regions of Australia (arid, tropical, coastal) to identify shared principles and context-specific practices
Investigate the Savanna Burning Carbon Farming Initiative as a case where traditional fire management is formally integrated with environmental markets
Research a specific Ranger group and evaluate how their dual knowledge system (cultural and ecological) functions in practice
Compare First Nations Australian custodial sustainability models with Māori kaitiakitanga in Aotearoa New Zealand, identifying structural parallels and differences
elaborations: identifying the influence of cultural values on how First Nations Australians manage environments (for example, continuity of cultural practices, management or development of Country/Place, and land tenure systems) and explaining custodial responsibilities for a Country/Place
discussing the role of First Nations Australian Park Rangers and their cultural knowledge and practices in the management of their Country/Place and environments

explaining First Nations Australians' models of sustainability, which contribute to broader conservation practices; for example, obligations to Country/Place, land management and care practices such as cleaning up the land and fire management, removal of weeds and rubbish, protection of threatened species, and capacity building within their communities

AC9HG10K04.minimum_width: Identify a specific environmental change context, describe its causes and impacts on at least one environmental function; identify at least two stakeholder perspectives on strategy development; propose and evaluate at least one management strategy against one criterion.
AC9HG10K04.typical_width: Describe causes and impacts of environmental change in a studied context; explain how world views influence stakeholders' strategy preferences; explain how Traditional Owners, communities, developers, governments and NGOs use environmental, economic and social criteria and consider trade-offs; propose and compare strategies using all three criteria; compare Australian management strategies with those in another country.
wider: Investigate a multi-scale case (local → national → global) tracing how the identified causes and effects change in character at each scale
Analyse a governance process (environmental impact assessment, resource management tribunal) to trace how different world views are weighted in formal decision-making
Evaluate a real implemented strategy over time using before/after evidence, identifying what was achieved and what remained unresolved
Investigate a case involving First Nations Traditional Owners where custodial management priorities diverged from government approaches, examining how tension was or was not resolved
elaborations: identifying a context to be studied, describing the causes of the environmental change and impacts for the sustainability of its functions (resource, service or spiritual)
recognising and discussing the influence of people's world views on how management strategies are developed and implemented

proposing strategies to manage the effects of environmental change; for example, environmental strategies – establishing marine reserves, national parks, World Heritage Sites or ecosystem-based management; spatial strategies – corridors to preserve flora and fauna or urban planning to reduce energy consumption; holistic thinking – addressing past and present causes of environmental change

comparing management strategies in Australia with strategies in another country for human-induced environmental change, using criteria; for example, managing waste in Australia compared with India's rubbish pickers or managing floods in Australia compared to floods in China
explaining how Traditional Owners, communities, developers, governments and non-government organisations use environmental, economic and social criteria, and consider trade-offs when making decisions

AC9HG10K05.minimum_width: Define human wellbeing as multi-dimensional; identify at least three SDGs relevant to wellbeing; compare GDP and at least one composite index (HDI or PQLI) for two countries and explain one difference in their rankings.
AC9HG10K05.typical_width: Identify SDGs relevant to human wellbeing; compare GDP, HDI and PQLI rankings for Australia, India and a Pacific country and explain trends in different measurements; interpret and explain trends in human wellbeing for a developed and a developing country over time.
wider: Evaluate composite measures such as MPI, Genuine Progress Indicator or Happy Planet Index against GDP and HDI, assessing what each adds
Investigate anomalies — countries that rank much higher on HDI than GDP (or vice versa) — and explain the political, historical or social factors that produce the divergence
Examine gender-disaggregated wellbeing data (GDI, GII) and evaluate what disaggregation reveals that composite indices obscure
Research how global shocks (pandemics, financial crises) differentially affect wellbeing trajectories in developed vs developing countries
elaborations: identifying the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 2015–2030 relevant to human wellbeing

comparing different measurements of human wellbeing (for example, comparing rankings of selected indicators such as Gross Domestic Product [GDP], Human Development Index [HDI] and Physical Quality of Life Index [PQLI] for Australia, India and a country in the Pacific) and explaining trends in the different measurements
interpreting and explaining trends in human wellbeing in a developed country and a developing country over time; for example, Australia compared with a country in Asia or the Pacific

AC9HG10K06.minimum_width: Interpret spatial wellbeing data for one country to describe the spatial pattern; identify at least two causes of the variation; describe at least two consequences of spatial inequality.
AC9HG10K06.typical_width: Interpret and analyse spatial data on wellbeing in India or another Asian country (e.g. using MPI or HDI sub-national data); identify regions of high and low wellbeing and explain similarities and differences (e.g. rural Rajasthan vs urban Mumbai); describe economic, social, technological, political and environmental causes; compare causes with those in Australia; interpret measures such as MPI, PFI and FSI to make inferences about wellbeing at different scales.
wider: Map multi-variable wellbeing data across subnational regions to identify spatial clustering patterns
Investigate how colonial history shaped current spatial inequalities within India — tracing how British infrastructure development produced long-lasting geographic economic concentrations
Examine intersectionality in causes — how caste, gender and geography interact in India to compound wellbeing disadvantage in specific regions
Compare feedback loops of spatial inequality between India and Australia — where low wellbeing produces further structural disadvantage
elaborations: interpreting and analysing measures of human wellbeing, and identifying and describing the causes and consequences of inequality
identifying and describing the economic, social, technological, political or environmental causes of variations in human wellbeing within India or another country compared to Australia

interpreting and analysing spatial data on human wellbeing in India or another country in Asia to identify the regions with high and low levels of human wellbeing, explaining similarities and differences; for example, rural Rajasthan compared to urban Mumbai

interpreting and analysing measures of human wellbeing, such as the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), Press Freedom Index (PFI) and Fragile States Index (FSI), and making inferences about the level of wellbeing at different scales; for example, for child labour and child slaves at the local scale or for Syria or Afghanistan at the national scale

AC9HG10K07.minimum_width: Describe wellbeing variation across at least two Australian places using data; identify at least two factors (from different domains) explaining the variation; explain how interconnections between at least two factors shape wellbeing in one specific place.
AC9HG10K07.typical_width: Interpret and analyse wellbeing data across urban, regional and remote Australian places including for First Nations Australians; explain environmental, social, economic and technological factors behind spatial variation; explain links between First Nations wellbeing data and Closing the Gap initiatives; explain how a person's wellbeing is influenced by place through interconnections of multiple factors in at least two different places.
wider: Investigate how historical policies (stolen generations, land alienation, forced relocation) created structural disadvantages that persist as causes of current wellbeing gaps for First Nations Australians
Examine wellbeing variation within the First Nations population — urban vs regional vs remote — avoiding national averages that obscure internal variation
Investigate and evaluate strategies proposed or implemented by First Nations communities themselves to improve wellbeing, assessing how community agency shapes outcomes
Compare how two government policy approaches to regional wellbeing (e.g. place-based investment vs targeted individual support) have fared in terms of outcomes
elaborations: explaining the environmental factors (access to resources – fossil fuels, water, fertile soils), the social factors (adequate food, health and education services), the economic factors (employment, income) and the technological factors (information and communications technology) that influence human wellbeing and development between and within countries

interpreting and analysing similarities, differences, patterns and trends in human wellbeing data for communities of First Nations Australians compared to non-Indigenous Australians, and explaining the links between human wellbeing and Closing the Gap initiatives

explaining how a person's wellbeing is influenced by where they live, with reference to interconnections of environmental, economic, social and technological factors in at least 2 different places in Australia, such as urban and remote places

AC9HG10K08.minimum_width: Describe the role of at least two different types of organisation (one government, one NGO) and identify objectives and outcomes of one specific program in at least one country context.
AC9HG10K08.typical_width: Identify and explain responses of government and NGO organisations to improve wellbeing in Australia (including First Nations programs), India or regional Pacific context; explain program objectives, outcomes and target populations; evaluate programs against stated objectives identifying effectiveness and limitations.
wider: Compare AusAID's approach with an equivalent bilateral aid agency (e.g. USAID, DFID/FCDO) — examining how different institutional mandates produce different program approaches
Examine community-proposed ways to improve First Nations wellbeing and compare these with government-initiated programs, identifying points of alignment and divergence
Apply a systematic evaluation framework (e.g. OECD-DAC criteria) to compare two programs in the same regional context
Investigate a program whose self-reported outcomes diverge from independent evaluation findings, examining what produces the gap
elaborations: identifying and describing a national, state or community program to reduce regional inequalities in human wellbeing in a country such as Papua New Guinea or Indonesia

explaining the objectives and outcomes of an overseas economic and social development program by the Australian Government (for example, AusAID) or a non-government overseas aid program (for example, World Vision) in India or a country in the Pacific
identifying and explaining ways to improve the wellbeing of remote communities of First Nations Australians, including ways proposed by the communities

AC9HG10S01.minimum_width: Generate at least three geographically framed questions about one phenomenon; modify at least one question to incorporate a geographical concept and specified scale; outline an investigation plan at two or more scales.
AC9HG10S01.typical_width: Develop a range of relevant questions addressing multiple dimensions of a phenomenon; modify and refine questions using geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnection, sustainability, scale, change) and scale of study; plan an investigation of a phenomenon at a range of scales using digital tools.
wider: Develop question sets for two contrasting phenomena and compare the inquiry structures, evaluating which questions are most productive for geographical investigation
Develop parallel versions of the same question at three different scales and explain how each calls for different data, methods and sources
Design an investigation plan where geospatial technologies are central to both data collection and analysis — not just presentation
Evaluate a completed geographical investigation plan for gaps in question coverage, scale consideration and data source selection
elaborations: developing a range of relevant questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or a challenge may arise; for example, 'What is human wellbeing?', 'How has human wellbeing changed over time?', 'How and why should inequality in human wellbeing be reduced?'

developing and modifying questions to sharpen the focus of an investigation using concepts or scale of study; for example, 'How are variations in the spatial distribution of human wellbeing measured at the global scale?', 'Why does human wellbeing vary between and within countries?' (national scale), 'How would you measure human wellbeing in the local area?' (local scale)

planning an investigation of a phenomenon or challenge being studied at a range of scales, using digital tools; for example, investigating the causes of human-induced climate change at the global scale and its impacts on Australia, Bangladesh and/or a Pacific Island country at the national scale

AC9HG10S02.minimum_width: Identify one primary research method appropriate to an inquiry; evaluate one source for at least two of the three criteria (relevance, reliability, bias); represent data from two variables using one digital tool.
AC9HG10S02.typical_width: Identify and use primary research methods including fieldwork; respect First Nations consultation protocols when relevant; evaluate primary and secondary sources for relevance, reliability and bias including information and selection bias; compare primary and secondary findings; represent multi-variable data using geospatial technologies and digital tools.
wider: Design and conduct a fieldwork-based investigation including choice of location, recording protocol and analysis
Analyse how bias operates differently in quantitative vs qualitative sources, developing a multi-type bias evaluation framework
Evaluate sources on First Nations community topics — examining power dynamics in what gets published and from whose perspective
Create a multi-panel visualisation combining geospatial mapping with statistical representations to tell a coherent geographical story
elaborations: identifying primary research methods, including fieldwork, to collect original materials; for example, survey and interviews regarding perspectives on environmental management at the local scale, or strategies to improve human wellbeing of First Nations Australians at the national and local scale

collecting relevant secondary research materials online using targeted criteria; for example, "allintext: critically endangered list by country" or "allintext: targets for reducing hunger or increasing access to health care"

identifying and respecting protocols for consultation with communities of First Nations Australians when planning and conducting investigations; for example, acknowledging their earth-centred world view and how their traditional knowledges contribute to environmental management projects, or considering cultural and spiritual wellbeing of First Nations Australians when implementing programs to reduce economic and social inequality

evaluating primary or secondary research materials for relevance (for example, "Does the information reflect current thinking?"), reliability (for example, "Who is/are the author/s? Does the author reference other experts in the field?") and bias, such as information bias presenting one side of an issue, or selection bias presenting information on the positive aspects of foreign aid with cultural and social issues not considered
comparing findings from primary research with those from secondary research materials for relevance and reliability

representing multi-variable data using geospatial technologies; for example, using scatterplots to visually represent data for countries to demonstrate the correlation between 2 variables, such as comparing adult literacy with GDP per capita in United Arab Emirates or Bhutan

representing multi-variable data using digital tools; for example, generating pie graphs showing threats to biodiversity; using digital photographs to indicate differences in material goods between people and places

AC9HG10S03.minimum_width: Develop at least one generalisation from geographical data that makes an inferential claim; identify a pattern and offer a causal explanation using at least one geographical factor; identify a likely relationship between two indicators.
AC9HG10S03.typical_width: Develop generalisations by critically analysing text and images for meaning and significance; explain patterns and trends in geographical data including trends in complex multi-variable datasets; infer relationships between key environmental or wellbeing indicators at the national scale using geospatial technology applications.
wider: Develop competing generalisations from the same dataset and evaluate which is better supported
Analyse contrasting satellite images or visual data to develop generalisations about what spatial contrast reveals at a geographical level
Examine how the apparent pattern changes with data aggregation scale — national vs subnational vs local for the same variable
Distinguish between correlation and causation in a geographical relationship, identifying cases where two indicators correlate but are both caused by a third factor
elaborations: developing generalisations; for example, critically analysing text and images for their meaning and significance, such as satellite images showing before and after deforestation in the Amazon or contrasting nightlife in North and South Korea

explaining patterns and trends; for example, explaining why a vegetation corridor for movement of koalas assists them to traverse through the bush and reduce death rates, or whether there has been an increased use of technology such as satellite images, drones and robots during and after a natural disaster to identify the need for aid

inferring relationships between key environmental indicators and sustainability of places at the national scale; for example, using a geospatial technologies application to create a map of Australia and another country to show measures of environmental change such as air quality, freshwater quality, fish resources, energy use, biodiversity or waste generation

AC9HG10S04.minimum_width: Draw a conclusion about a geographical phenomenon using at least two named geographical concepts as organisers; evaluate whether the reasons given for one conclusion adequately justify it.
AC9HG10S04.typical_width: Draw conclusions using at least two geographical concepts as analytical organisers (not just labels); examine the reasons given for specific decisions related to sustainability or wellbeing and explain how these have or have not justified the conclusion reached; identify where interconnected factors (environmental, economic, social, political, technological) are accounted for or overlooked.
wider: Compare conclusions drawn when using different concept pairings for the same data, evaluating how concept selection shapes analytical direction
Construct an alternative conclusion from the same data and evidence, explaining what different reasoning steps would be required
Evaluate a geographical decision from a policy document — tracing explicit and implicit reasoning, identifying assumptions and assessing whether the conclusion follows from the evidence
Investigate a decision that was later revised and examine what new evidence or reasoning caused the revision
elaborations: drawing conclusions using at least 2 concepts, such as place, space, environment, interconnection, sustainability, scale and change as organisers for example discussing the concept of sustainability in relation to human-induced change affecting environments or considering implications of spatial variations in human wellbeing

examining the reasons given for making a specific decision and explain how these reasons have or have not justified the conclusion reached, such as considering the interconnection of environmental, economic, social, political or technological factors when developing strategies to address sustainable management of environments, or unequal access of people to resources essential for human wellbeing

AC9HG10S05.minimum_width: Propose at least one individual and one collective strategy for a geographical challenge; evaluate one strategy against at least two criteria; recommend one strategy with at least two predicted impacts and one reflection on personal values.
AC9HG10S05.typical_width: Develop and evaluate individual and collective strategies for environmental or wellbeing challenges; evaluate strategies using environmental, economic and social criteria including First Nations traditional practices; recommend a strategy with explained predicted impacts; reflect on personal values and how they influence strategy choices.
wider: Compare scale and type of impact achievable through individual vs collective action for the same challenge
Research a case where grassroots collective action led to policy change, tracing the pathway from individual decisions to systems-level impact
Apply a systematic multi-criteria framework to compare two strategies, producing a reasoned recommendation that explicitly addresses trade-offs
Apply sustainable design principles to an urban redevelopment strategy and explain how the principles reflect specific values about wellbeing, environment and community
elaborations: proposing individual action and supporting the strategy with reasons; for example, reducing their ecological footprint by reducing the amount of food packaging included in a packed lunch, or becoming volunteers for non-government organisations such as the Red Cross or Red Crescent to increase social connectedness

proposing collective action and evaluation of actions; for example, identifying ways to improve the wellbeing of remote communities of First Nations Australians and evaluating the actions proposed and implemented by the community members

evaluating the effectiveness of a strategy in relation to environmental, economic or social criteria; for example, reflecting on whether environment degradation has been reduced and human wellbeing improved

explaining reasons for decisions and choices, such as the traditional use of firestick farming by First Nations Australians to control fires, or grassroots decisions on implementation and effectiveness of aid projects

reflecting on personal values and attitudes and how these influence strategies; for example, applying sustainable design principles to urban redevelopment projects that provide green, open spaces for citizens, or supporting non-government organisations that reflect personal values

AC9HG10S06.minimum_width: Produce a structured response with at least two structural features; include at least one geospatial or digital tool output with accurate geographical concepts and terms acknowledged from research; demonstrate an identifiable tone appropriate to the stated purpose.
AC9HG10S06.typical_width: Create descriptions, explanations and responses using structural features (sub-headings, logical sequencing) for a specific purpose; present conclusions using geospatial technologies and digital tools incorporating accurate concepts and terms; develop explanations using authoritative tone appropriate to purpose and audience, referring to data representations and research findings.
wider: Produce two versions of the same content using different structural approaches for different audiences — explaining the structural differences and why they serve each audience
Produce the same content with two different tones for two different audiences, evaluating how vocabulary, sentence structure and hedging language shift
Analyse how geospatial data representations are integrated into the structure of a professional geographical report — evaluating their argumentative function not just their illustrative role
Design and produce a multi-panel data visualisation that combines geospatial mapping with statistical representations to tell a coherent geographical story
elaborations: creating a description for a purpose, using structural features to organise ideas, findings, impacts and actions; for example, sub-headings

presenting conclusions using geospatial technologies and digital tools to create representations of data (for example, the trends in Human Development Index [HDI] over time in a selected country or region) and research findings (for example, how a person's wellbeing is influenced by where they live) to explain causes and effects of a geographical phenomenon or challenge, and reinforcing understanding of the interconnections between people, places and the environment

developing an explanation, applying tone appropriate to purpose and audience; for example, using an authoritative tone, and referring to representations of data and information when explaining a strategy to improve the sustainability of an identified environment or action to improve human wellbeing
